articles.description:
We needed to publish four manuscripts (43,699 bytes in total) that another project had handed over, and the obvious move was to ask an LLM to turn the markdown into HTML. We wrote a deterministic converter instead. It used zero LLM tokens, extracted 23 FAQ questions automatically, and all four posts passed its built-in checks. The reason is not cost. The manuscripts already contained values that had been cross-checked by hand, such as notice numbers and page numbers, so changing a single character during formatting would itself be a defect.
This post covers the rule we use to decide between a script and an LLM, what the converter actually does, and the two publishing traps it closed without anyone having to remember them.

Ask these about the step you are about to automate. A single "yes" …
articles.title: Markdown to HTML: 0 LLM Tokens for 4 Posts, 23 FAQs Extracted

articles.author: GeoImageTagger
articles.description:
If you have ever run images through a compression pipeline and discovered the EXIF data came out empty, the explanation is usually straightforward: the compressor never handled the metadata in the first place.
Image compression operates on pixel data. Metadata — EXIF, IPTC, XMP, GPS coordinates — is stored in structurally separate sections of the file. Whether those sections survive compression is entirely a function of how the tool is built.
JPEG files use marker segments to organize data. The pixel stream starts at the SOS (Start of Scan) marker. Metadata lives in application markers:
APP1 (0xFFE1) — EXIF and XMP payloads
APP13 (0xFFED) — IPTC-IIM data
APP2 (0xFFE2) — ICC color profiles
Low-level libraries like libjpeg and libjpeg-turbo process only the pixel buffer. They do not automati…
articles.title: Why Image Compressors Strip Metadata — and How to Prevent It

Quick answer: On a low-memory machine, the lightest real option is a terminal client such as curl, HTTPie, or xh, followed by a native or Tauri-based desktop GUI. The popular Electron clients bundle a full Chromium runtime per install and usually hold the largest resident set. Treat every memory figure as something you measure yourself, since idle RAM, a large collection, and several open tabs move the number more than the product name does.
Two clients can show the same request builder and still cost very different amounts of memory. The difference is usually the runtime underneath. An Electron app ships its own Chromium and Node, then splits work across a main process, a renderer, and a few GPU and utility helpers. That keeps the app consistent across systems, but each helper stays resid…

The page as markdown with numbered elements; it clicks and types by number.

Console and network reads for testing your app on localhost.
